description:
ChronoNauts is a team of innovators exploring the future of space exploration through AI, physics, and engineering. We are developing TIMEFLIGHT AI, an interactive space mission simulator that explores relativistic time dilation, spacecraft trajectories, and mission optimization. Our goal is to turn complex scientific concepts into an engaging tool that helps people understand the possibilities and challenges of future space travel.

Explore. Optimize. Travel Beyond Time. 🚀
summary: TIMEFLIGHT AI: Relativistic Mission Simulator is an interactive, game-like simulator that makes the trade-offs between spacecraft speed, crew time, and idealized energy easier to explore. Users choose a destination, cruise speed, spacecraft mass, and one-way or return travel. The app compares elapsed time on Earth and aboard the spacecraft, estimates relativistic kinetic energy, and visualizes the results with charts and animated clocks. Its NASA/JPL Horizons feature retrieves planetary state vectors and derives current Earth-to-planet distance and a rough travel-time estimate. This educational prototype assumes constant cruise speed; it does not model real propulsion, acceleration phases, or planetary interception.
details:
High-level project summary

TIMEFLIGHT AI is an interactive, game-like educational simulator that makes one difficult mission-design trade-off tangible: how cruise speed changes the time experienced by a crew and the idealized kinetic energy required by a spacecraft. Users choose a nearby-star destination or custom distance, cruise velocity, spacecraft mass, and one-way or return travel. The dashboard compares Earth-frame and crew-frame time, estimates relativistic kinetic energy, and visualizes the route with animated clocks and a speed-responsive spacecraft.

An optional NASA/JPL Horizons feature retrieves current Earth-centered state vectors for Mars, Venus, Jupiter, or Saturn. TIMEFLIGHT AI derives the body's current distance and relative speed and shows a clearly labeled, simplified cruise-time estimate. The prototype helps learners experiment with mission parameters and understand why speed has consequences. It focuses on relativistic time and energy; it is not a complete mission-optimization game or a flight-planning tool.

Detailed project description

TIMEFLIGHT AI is a Streamlit-based educational mission simulator focused on special-relativistic time dilation. The user configures a nearby-star destination or custom distance, cruise speed as a fraction of the speed of light, spacecraft mass, nominal acceleration, and whether the route is one-way or a return trip.

The simulator calculates Earth-frame travel time from distance and cruise speed. It calculates the Lorentz factor, γ = 1 / √(1 − v²/c²), and estimates crew-frame elapsed time as Earth time divided by γ. It estimates ideal relativistic kinetic energy per burn using K = (γ − 1)mc², then counts acceleration/deceleration burns for the selected trip. A Plotly chart compares Earth and crew time across cruise speeds. The interface also includes an illustrative route animation and clock-rate animation. Rule-based mission notes flag selected speed, acceleration, energy, or duration considerations.

The optional NASA/JPL Horizons panel requests state vectors for Mars, Venus, Jupiter, or Saturn relative to Earth. It displays the returned rows and derives current separation and relative speed from the first vector. Using the selected cruise speed, it then estimates Earth and crew travel times. This planetary estimate assumes the target remains at its current position; it does not calculate an intercept.

The prototype makes the relationship between speed, elapsed time, and ideal kinetic energy accessible through direct experimentation. Its calculations assume constant cruise speed and instantaneous acceleration/deceleration. The acceleration slider affects guidance only. The model omits propulsion efficiency, fuel, budgets, instruments, launch vehicles, power, communications, orbital mechanics, radiation, and life support. Mission guidance is deterministic and rule-based; it is not a trained AI model. The simulator is educational and is not suitable for real mission planning.

Technology: Python, Streamlit, Plotly, Requests, and NASA/JPL Horizons API.

We used a generative AI assistant (OpenAI/Copilot) to assist with Python/Streamlit implementation, debugging, interface refinement, and editing project descriptions. The ChronoNauts team supplied the project concept and challenge direction and reviewed the AI-assisted output. Mission recommendations in the app are rule-based, not generated by an AI model. NASA/JPL measurements are fetched from the Horizons API and are not AI-generated. No AI-generated images, video, or audio are included in this submission.

The project uses the NASA/JPL Horizons API (https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/api/horizons.api) to request Earth-centered state vectors for Mars (499), Venus (299), Jupiter (599), or Saturn (699). The app requests vectors for the current date and the following day. It displays the returned data and uses the first row to derive current Earth-to-body separation and relative speed, then estimates a constant-cruise travel time using the user's selected speed. This estimate does not model the target's future motion or an orbital intercept. The interstellar-star distances in the main mission designer are fixed approximate values in the app and are not obtained from Horizons.

Space Agency Partner data and other references

  • NASA/JPL Horizons API: https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/api/horizons.api
  • NASA Space Apps 2026 challenge, Space Mission Design Game: https://www.spaceappschallenge.org/2026/challenges/space-mission-design-game/
  • Python: https://www.python.org/
  • Streamlit: https://streamlit.io/
  • Plotly: https://plotly.com/python/
  • Requests: https://requests.readthedocs.io/
  • Nearby-star distances are approximate constants in app.py; add the team's chosen astronomical source for these values before submission if the form expects every data source to be individually cited.
  • No NASA logos, NASA imagery, or third-party photographs are used in the deck.

Seven-slide demo outline

The editable slide deck is TIMEFLIGHT_AI_7_Slides.pptx.

  1. TIMEFLIGHT AI — ChronoNauts, challenge name, and the core promise: make relativistic mission trade-offs tangible.
  2. The challenge — Mission trade-offs are abstract; the prototype focuses on speed, crew time, and energy.
  3. A mission-design experience — Choose a route and spacecraft settings; compare the calculated outcomes.
  4. One scenario, two clocks — Proxima Centauri at 80% of c: about 10.62 Earth years, 6.37 crew years, γ ≈ 1.67, and about 6.7 million TWh of idealized round-trip energy for a 100,000 kg craft.
  5. NASA/JPL data in the loop — Explain the live Horizons vectors and the derived present-distance estimate, separately from the interstellar route model.
  6. The trade-off — Faster cruise reduces elapsed time but increases ideal kinetic energy sharply.
  7. Impact and next steps — Educational value, honest model limits, and future work toward budgets, payloads, and target-motion-aware trajectories.
